asDecan.p: Each sign is split into three ten-degree slices, called decans, each with a ruling planet and a small card. Your Sun sits between 20 and 29 degrees of Gemini, the last slice, and in the old Chaldean order that one goes to the Sun itself. The Sun has no special dignity in Gemini. It's a visitor, neither helped nor held back, so it takes on the tone of Mercury, who owns the sign. So your Sun is sitting in the one slice of Gemini the Sun runs, and I've seen that make people here surer of themselves than earlier Geminis. The first slice is the Eight of Swords, Jupiter's, and the middle is the Nine, Mars's, the one lying awake at three in the morning. Yours comes after both. The picture looks grim, I know, but have a look at the strip of gold along the horizon. The Lovers is your Sun card and this is the finer grain inside it, close enough to Cancer that home matters more than people expect of a Gemini.

You tend to think things through to the very end, out loud, usually to someone. A friend mentions their landlord's put the rent up and by the time the coffee's finished you've walked them through the whole thing, the letter they should send, what happens if he says no, where they'd move and how long the commute would be. In a work meeting you're the one asking where this actually ends up while everyone else is still on slide three. When a text sits on read for an afternoon, you've written the complete story of why, with an ending, before dinner. And then, which is the part people miss, you're done with it. The Sun here likes a conclusion. Loose ends bother you far more than bad news does, and a Sunday with nothing planned usually goes on tying them off, returning the parcel, answering the email you've been avoiding, ringing your mum back.

The less obvious gift is that you can say a thing is over, mean it, and have people believe you. A project at work has been limping along for eight months, everyone's still putting hours in because nobody wants to be the one, and you're the one who says in the meeting that it isn't going to work and explains why. It lands because you've clearly thought it all the way through. The same happens with friends. Someone rings you at eleven at night halfway through a break-up and you let them tell you the whole thing, the worst version, every bit of it. Somewhere near the end they hear themselves and feel lighter, because every corner of it has been looked at and there's nothing left lurking. You also get up quickly after your own setbacks, quicker than most, and that steadies the people around you.

The less obvious shadow is calling time too early. You run a story to its last page so fast that you sometimes decide something's finished when it only needed one hard conversation. A flatmate leaves the kitchen in a state twice and in your head the arrangement's already over, you've looked at other flats, and they haven't a clue anything's wrong. A job has one bad quarter and there's a resignation letter sitting in your notes app. There's a second thing too. You tell a good story, you're a Gemini, and bad things make the best stories, so the disaster gets told at dinner and told again and gets a little bigger each time. After a while you're more attached to the version where it all went wrong than to what happened, and the people who were there start to notice the two don't quite match.

When something really goes wrong, a redundancy, a friend falling out with you, a parent going into hospital, the first thing you do is talk. You ring three people in one evening and tell each of them the whole thing, and every time it gets clearer and a bit worse. You're up late looking things up, the worst outcome, then the second worst. About a week later there's usually a strange calm. You've decided it's the end of something and you've already started on what comes next, which can look very sudden from outside. The cost lands on whoever's still upset. Your partner is still grieving the old plan while you're on to the new one, and they can feel left behind on the ground. What actually helps is sleep, a walk without your phone, and letting one person be sad about it with you for longer than feels useful.

You need a conversation to finish. An argument left hanging overnight is close to unbearable, so you'll follow your partner from room to room at midnight trying to get to the end of it, and someone who needs to go quiet and think it over can find that exhausting. It's worth knowing that about yourself. There's also more of a homebody in you than people expect from a Gemini, that's the Cancer edge of these degrees, and the partner who gets to see it gets a very loyal person. When a relationship does end you tend to end it properly. No getting back together three times, no hovering around each other's lives online. You've said why and you go. Exes sometimes find that cold. Usually it means you did most of the grieving while it was still going, quietly, in your own head.

The Lovers as your Sun card is about choosing, and this slice is good at the choice nobody else wants to make. You tend to do well where the job is finishing things or explaining bad news clearly. Editing, where most of the work is cutting. Project close-outs and post-mortems. Crisis communications, turnaround work, insolvency, being the manager sent in to wind a team down decently. Journalism, especially anything with a hard deadline and a final version. You're very good at the last ten per cent of a job, the stretch where everything has to be pulled together and said plainly. The risk is getting known as the person who kills things and being handed only the grim jobs. Tell your manager you'd like to start something as well, and take the next new project when it's offered, even a small one.

At twenty this decan often looks like a lot of dramatic endings. Friendships finished over one bad night, a course dropped in week three, a break-up announced to the whole group before the other person has quite caught up. Everything feels final because you can see where it's heading so quickly. By the mid-thirties most people with a Sun here have been wrong about an ending or two, and it softens them. They still see the end of the road early, and they're more willing to walk a bit further before deciding. They usually have a rough year or two behind them as well, and know from experience that they got up again. The fifties tend to bring the Cancer side forward, the house, the family, the friends who stuck around. A lot of them become the person others ring in the worst month of their lives, and they're calm and plain-spoken and good at it.

When you catch yourself on the last page of a worst-case story, the email you've decided means you're being let go, the quiet you've decided means the relationship's over, write the story down in three lines. Underneath, write what you actually know for certain, which is usually one line. Leave both on the page for a day before you act on either or say anything to anyone. Most of the time the second list is shorter and duller, and that's the one to go on.
